**Title: "Google’s Hidden Tracking Feature Sparks Privacy Concerns"**

In a startling revelation, Google has confirmed that its Android system was collecting location data from users even when they had disabled location services and removed their SIM cards—a feature that raised serious privacy concerns. According to a report by *Quartz*, Google’s messaging service had been requesting the unique addresses of nearby mobile phone masts, known as Cell IDs, since early 2017. This data, transmitted by modern Android devices, allowed Google to track users’ locations with surprising accuracy, despite their efforts to protect their privacy.

A Google spokesperson acknowledged the issue, stating that the company had explored using Cell IDs to improve the speed and performance of message delivery through its Firebase Cloud Messaging service. However, they claimed the data was never stored and that the feature was quickly removed. "We never incorporated Cell ID into our network sync system, so that data was immediately discarded," the spokesperson said. Yet, privacy advocates argue that the mere collection of such data—even temporarily—violates users’ reasonable expectations of privacy.

The controversy centers on how Google’s service, designed to ensure reliable message delivery, inadvertently became a tracking tool. By analyzing the Cell ID alongside the mobile country code and network code, Google could pinpoint a user’s location within a 400-meter radius—sometimes even more precisely in densely populated areas. This level of detail, achieved through triangulation, mirrors the same technology used when location services are actively enabled.

As public backlash grows, Google faces pressure to return to more transparent data practices. Critics argue that while the company may have discarded the Cell ID data, the incident highlights a troubling pattern of overreach in the name of service optimization. Meanwhile, advertisers and third-party apps, which rely on Google’s ad-targeting capabilities, may have benefited from this hidden tracking feature, further fueling concerns about corporate surveillance.

For now, users are left questioning whether their privacy can ever truly be protected in an era where even the most basic features of their devices can be exploited for tracking. Google’s swift removal of the Cell ID collection suggests an attempt to mitigate damage, but the incident has already left a lasting mark on the public’s trust.
